name: Alanyl-glutamine

lead: Alanyl-glutamine is a synthetic dipeptide of alanine and glutamine, made so glutamine can be given in a stable, water-soluble form. Some lifters consider it for muscle recovery and holding on to muscle.

Given intravenously, the dipeptide supplies glutamine to tissues. A 1989 Lancet trial of 12 patients after colorectal surgery examined muscle glutamine loss and nitrogen balance, and later research covered surgery, trauma, critical illness and gut disease. Results vary, including a randomized study that found no benefit in autologous transplant patients. No trials target muscle growth or appearance in healthy people.

paras: Lifters use it as a powder mixed into drinks, typically around training, in the same slot as ordinary glutamine. Clinical use is as part of hospital nutrition.
Reported trials are in hospital patients and results vary. No safety data from healthy-lifter use appear in the reference material.

angle.text: Alanyl-glutamine is a stable glutamine dipeptide that some lifters consider for faster recovery and keeping more muscle. Its research is in hospital nutrition, such as muscle glutamine loss after surgery.

lead: Alanyl-glutamine (L-alanyl-L-glutamine) is a synthetic dipeptide used as a glutamine source in clinical nutrition. A 1989 randomized Lancet study in 12 patients after colorectal cancer surgery gave it in parenteral nutrition and examined muscle glutamine loss and nitrogen balance.[1]

Research since then has covered surgery, trauma, critical illness, intestinal disease, infection and malnutrition.[2][3][4] The reference material contains no trials of alanyl-glutamine for muscle gain or appearance in healthy people.
infobox: Intravenous (clinical); oral studied in some trials

paras: The 1989 Lancet study reported on muscle glutamine loss and nitrogen balance after major surgery in patients given the dipeptide versus a control regimen.[1] A related 1990 study examined whether it counteracted depletion of free glutamine and the postoperative decline in muscle protein synthesis.[5] A 1999 randomized, double-blind study of 120 postoperative patients examined clinical safety, nitrogen balance and intestinal permeability.[6]

A 2006 study in multiple-trauma patients reported that parenteral alanyl-glutamine prevented worsening of insulin sensitivity.[7] In contrast, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study titled as such concluded that standardized parenteral alanyl-glutamine was not beneficial in autologous transplant patients.[8]

Registered trials include studies in pressure ulcers in critically ill patients, Clostridioides difficile infection, and childhood malnutrition and enteropathy.[9][10] No study in the reference material tests it for physique outcomes in healthy people.

timeline.event: Randomized study of parenteral alanyl-glutamine after major surgery published in The Lancet.[1]
